scenarios.depth_note: First-time employer payroll tax setup: EIN, withholding, FICA, state unemployment, deposit schedules
scenarios.prompt: I just formed an LLC and I'm hiring my first full-time employee at $65,000 salary starting November 1st. Walk me through every payroll tax obligation: getting an EIN, federal income tax withholding, FICA, federal and state unemployment insurance, and whether I deposit monthly or semi-weekly. I'm in Texas. Give me the actual deadlines and what happens if I mess this up.

scenarios.depth_note: Multi-state payroll compliance: nexus, reciprocal agreements, registration in employee's state
scenarios.prompt: My LLC is in Illinois but I just hired a remote designer who lives in Colorado at $8,000/month. Do I need to register for payroll taxes in Colorado? Explain state withholding, unemployment insurance, and whether Illinois and Colorado have a reciprocal agreement. What are the penalties if I just keep running her through Illinois payroll?

scenarios.depth_note: IRS misclassification risk assessment: behavioral/financial control tests and penalties
scenarios.prompt: I've had a 'contractor' working 40 hours a week for me for 18 months. I set her hours, she uses my laptop, she can't work for anyone else, and I pay her $7,500/month on a 1099. Be honest: how likely is it the IRS would reclassify her as an employee, and what would the back taxes and penalties actually cost me?

scenarios.depth_note: Contractor-to-employee conversion cost modeling: loaded cost, benefits, payroll taxes
scenarios.prompt: I'm converting my top contractor ($120,000/year on 1099) to a W-2 employee. Calculate the true loaded cost: employer FICA, unemployment insurance, workers comp, plus a basic benefits package (health insurance stipend, 15 days PTO, 401k match). What salary keeps my total cost neutral, and what do I legally owe her that I didn't before?

scenarios.depth_note: Piercing the corporate veil: commingling consequences and remediation steps
scenarios.prompt: I formed an LLC last year but I've been running everything through my personal checking account — about $180,000 in business revenue mixed with personal spending. Explain piercing the corporate veil in plain terms: how exposed am I really, and give me the exact cleanup steps including what accounts to open and how to document the past mess.

scenarios.depth_note: Owner draw vs salary tax treatment in LLCs and S-corps, self-employment tax optimization
scenarios.prompt: My single-member LLC nets about $160,000/year. I've just been transferring money to myself whenever I need it. Should I be taking owner draws or putting myself on salary? Show me the self-employment tax math both ways and tell me at what income level electing S-corp status starts paying off.

scenarios.depth_note: S-corp quarterly estimated tax calculation with reasonable salary requirement
scenarios.prompt: I'm an S-corp owner with $180,000 in net business income this year. I pay myself a $90,000 salary. Calculate my quarterly estimated tax payments: what's the safe harbor amount based on last year's $22,000 total tax, when are the four deadlines, and how do I split between the salary withholding and the quarterly payments on the pass-through income?

scenarios.depth_note: Missed estimated payments: underpayment penalties, annualized income method, catch-up strategy
scenarios.prompt: I forgot to make my Q1 and Q2 estimated tax payments as an S-corp owner — I owe roughly $14,000 per quarter and we're now in October. What's the underpayment penalty going to cost me, can I use the annualized income installment method to reduce it since most of my income came in Q3, and what's my best catch-up move right now?

scenarios.depth_note: Business card selection for high ad spend: rewards math, fees, APR comparison
scenarios.prompt: My digital agency spends about $40,000/year on Facebook and Google ads plus $15,000 on software subscriptions. Compare the top 3 business credit cards for this spend profile — show me the actual dollar value of rewards minus annual fees, and flag which ones report to personal credit bureaus versus only business.

scenarios.depth_note: Building business credit from zero: secured cards, EIN-only tradelines, timeline
scenarios.prompt: I just started my LLC and have no business credit history. My personal credit is 720. Give me a 12-month plan to build a business credit profile from scratch: which cards to get first, whether to use my SSN or EIN, how Dun & Bradstreet factors in, and when I'll realistically qualify for a real business line of credit.

scenarios.depth_note: Collections escalation ladder: reminders, late fees, demand letters, collections agencies, legal action
scenarios.prompt: A client owes me $18,000 and we're at 90 days past due. I've sent two polite reminders. Give me the full escalation ladder: exactly what to say and when, when to add late fees, when to send a formal demand letter, at what point a collections agency makes sense (and what they'll take), and when small claims versus regular court is the right call.

scenarios.depth_note: Preventive invoice terms design: deposits, net terms, late-fee clauses, kill fees
scenarios.prompt: I'm done chasing late payments. I'm rewriting my standard invoice terms for $10k-$50k projects. Design the terms for me: what deposit percentage, net-15 vs net-30, late fee structure that's enforceable, and what contract language lets me pause work when payment is late. Make it firm but not client-repelling.

scenarios.depth_note: Retainer break-even math: effective hourly rate, utilization risk, scope boundaries
scenarios.prompt: I bill $150/hour as a freelancer and a client wants me on a $4,000/month retainer for roughly 25 hours of work monthly. Do the math: what's my effective hourly rate, how many hours can I actually work before I lose money versus hourly, and what contract language protects me if they start demanding 40 hours?

scenarios.depth_note: Mid-contract retainer renegotiation when scope has expanded beyond original terms
scenarios.prompt: I'm 4 months into a $5,000/month retainer that was scoped at 20 hours, but the client is consistently using 35+ hours and treating me like a full-time employee. I don't want to lose them — they're $60k/year in revenue. Give me a renegotiation plan: the data to bring, how to frame the conversation, and 3 restructuring options with pricing.

scenarios.depth_note: E&O and general liability procurement for enterprise contracts: limits, exclusions, cost
scenarios.prompt: I just landed an enterprise consulting contract that requires $2M in errors & omissions insurance and $1M/$2M general liability before I can start. I've never bought business insurance. What exactly do I need to buy, what will it cost annually for a solo consultant, what exclusions should I watch for, and how fast can I get certificates issued?

scenarios.depth_note: Home-based business coverage gaps: homeowner's exclusions, equipment, liability
scenarios.prompt: I run my LLC from a home office with about $25,000 in computer and video equipment, and clients occasionally visit. Does my homeowner's policy cover any of this if there's a fire or if a client gets hurt? Identify the specific gaps and tell me the cheapest way to fill them — rider, in-home business policy, or BOP.

scenarios.depth_note: Simplified vs actual expense method: side-by-side math for a real office footprint
scenarios.prompt: I have a dedicated 300 sq ft home office in a 2,000 sq ft house. My annual home expenses: $24,000 mortgage interest and taxes, $3,600 utilities, $2,400 insurance, $18,000 rent equivalent if I rented. Calculate my deduction under the simplified method versus the actual expense method, and tell me which wins and by how much.

scenarios.depth_note: Audit risk and documentation: what triggers IRS scrutiny, exclusive-use tests, recordkeeping
scenarios.prompt: I want to claim the home office deduction but I'm worried about getting audited. What actually triggers IRS scrutiny on home office claims, how strict is the exclusive-and-regular-use test really, and what documentation should I keep so I can defend a $4,000 deduction without breaking a sweat?

scenarios.depth_note: Contribution limit comparison at $200k profit: which vehicle maximizes deductible contributions
scenarios.prompt: I'm a solo founder with $200,000 in net self-employment profit and no employees. Compare SEP-IRA versus Solo 401(k) with real numbers: maximum deductible contribution under each, the deadlines to set up and fund for this tax year, and whether the Solo 401(k)'s Roth option changes the answer.

scenarios.depth_note: Plan transition when hiring: Solo 401k disqualification, SEP coverage rules, alternatives
scenarios.prompt: I have a Solo 401(k) with $150,000 in it and I'm about to hire my first full-time employee. I know the Solo 401(k) dies when I hire. Walk me through exactly what happens: the deadline to act, whether I convert to a SEP-IRA or a regular 401(k), what it costs to cover the new employee, and how to avoid a compliance disaster.

scenarios.depth_note: Reserve sizing from monthly burn: months of coverage, where to park it, tiering
scenarios.prompt: My agency burns $35,000/month in payroll and overhead, with revenue swinging between $40k and $70k monthly. How big should my business emergency fund be, where exactly should I park it (and what yield can I get while keeping it liquid), and how do I rebuild it after I have to dip in?

scenarios.depth_note: Seasonal revenue reserve modeling: sizing for concentrated income periods
scenarios.prompt: My business makes 70% of its $400,000 annual revenue in Q4 (holiday retail) but expenses run $25,000/month year-round. Model my cash flow month by month, tell me exactly how much I need banked by September to survive Q1-Q3, and how to handle the temptation to overspend when Q4 cash floods in.

scenarios.depth_note: Contract review for $50k project: IP ownership, payment terms, termination, liability caps
scenarios.prompt: A client sent me their standard contract for a $50,000 project. Review it like a lawyer would: IP ownership and work-for-hire language, payment schedule and late remedies, termination for convenience terms, liability caps and indemnification, and non-compete clauses. Tell me the 5 clauses most likely to hurt me and the exact redlines to push back with.

scenarios.depth_note: Kill fee and cancellation clause design: protecting against mid-project termination
scenarios.prompt: A client just cancelled a $30,000 project 3 weeks in after I'd turned down other work. My contract had no kill fee. Draft a cancellation/kill-fee clause for my future contracts: what percentage at what milestones, how to handle work already performed, and how to make it enforceable without scaring clients off.

scenarios.depth_note: Change-order process design: intake, pricing, approval workflow, client communication
scenarios.prompt: Every project I do gets hit with 'just one small thing' requests that add up to weeks of unbilled work. Design a complete change-order process for me: how to spot scope creep in the moment, a simple change-request form, how to price extras (hourly vs fixed), and the exact script for telling a client 'that's outside scope' without damaging the relationship.

scenarios.depth_note: Retroactive recovery of unbilled scope: how to bill for work already performed
scenarios.prompt: I already did about $8,000 worth of out-of-scope work for a client over the last 2 months without a change order — I just said yes to everything. The project isn't over yet. Is there any way to recover this money now, or do I eat it? Give me a realistic playbook for the conversation and what to do differently on the remaining work.

scenarios.depth_note: Financial impact analysis of firing a major client: revenue concentration, replacement timeline
scenarios.prompt: My worst client is 40% of my revenue ($96,000/year) — constantly late paying, abusive to work with, scope creeps everything. Model the financial impact of firing them: my true margin on their work after the hassle factor, how many months of runway I have, and how long it'll realistically take to replace that revenue with better clients.

scenarios.depth_note: Professional offboarding execution: transition plan, final invoice, referral handoff
scenarios.prompt: I've decided to fire a $6,000/month retainer client. Give me the execution plan: the exact email to send, how much notice to give, how to transition their work without burning the bridge, how to handle the final invoice and any prepaid work, and whether to refer them to someone else.

scenarios.depth_note: Churn modeling and grandfathering strategy for a 20% across-the-board increase
scenarios.prompt: I haven't raised prices in 3 years and I need to go up 20% across 8 retainer clients ($4k-$8k/month each). Model the churn risk: if I lose 1-2 clients, am I still ahead? Should I grandfather anyone, stagger the increases, or rip the band-aid off? Give me a tiered rollout plan.

scenarios.depth_note: Price-increase client communication: messaging, timing, objection handling
scenarios.prompt: Write the actual price-increase email for my retainer clients — I'm going from $5,000 to $6,000/month. It needs to go out next week. Give me the full draft, the best day/time to send it, how to handle the client who immediately threatens to leave, and what concession (if any) I should have ready.

scenarios.depth_note: Credit facility selection for $75k expansion: cost comparison, qualification, covenants
scenarios.prompt: I need $75,000 to expand my business — new equipment and a hire. Compare a business line of credit versus a term loan for this: true cost of each over 3 years, what banks actually require to qualify (revenue, time in business, credit score), and which one fits a 6-month spend timeline better. My business does $500k/year revenue.

scenarios.depth_note: Revolving credit discipline: draw/repay management, avoiding a permanent balance
scenarios.prompt: I have a $50,000 business line of credit that I've been using to smooth cash flow, but the balance never goes below $30,000 and I'm paying $400/month in interest. Give me a system to manage draws and repayments: rules for when to draw, a paydown schedule, and how to tell if I'm using it as intended versus masking a profitability problem.

scenarios.depth_note: Buy vs lease analysis for $60k equipment: Section 179, total cost, flexibility
scenarios.prompt: I need $60,000 in commercial kitchen equipment for my catering business. Compare buying with an equipment loan versus leasing for 5 years: total out-of-pocket cost, Section 179 deduction treatment for each, what happens to the equipment at the end, and which makes sense if I might upgrade in 3 years.

scenarios.depth_note: End-of-lease decision math: buyout vs return vs upgrade
scenarios.prompt: My 5-year equipment lease is ending in 4 months. The buyout is $12,000, the equipment is worth about $15,000 used, and the dealer is offering me new equipment on a fresh lease. Do the math on buyout vs return vs upgrade, including the tax treatment of each option.

scenarios.depth_note: Processing statement audit: interchange-plus vs flat rate, hidden fees, negotiation leverage
scenarios.prompt: I'm paying 3.5% all-in on $500,000/year in card volume through my current processor — that's $17,500/year. Audit this for me: what should I actually be paying on interchange-plus, which junk fees to look for on my statement, and give me a negotiation script to take to my processor or a competitor quote.

scenarios.depth_note: Surcharging vs cash discount legality and customer impact by state
scenarios.prompt: I'm thinking about adding a 3% credit card surcharge or a cash discount program to offset my processing fees. Is surcharging legal in my state, what are the Visa/Mastercard disclosure rules, and honestly — how do customers react? Give me the compliance requirements and the real-world impact on sales.

scenarios.depth_note: Multi-state nexus determination for Shopify sellers: economic thresholds, registration steps
scenarios.prompt: I sell online through Shopify and shipped to 12 states last year totaling $380,000 in sales. Where do I likely have sales tax nexus based on economic thresholds, what are the registration steps in the 3 highest-risk states, and what's the penalty exposure if I've been ignoring this for 2 years?

scenarios.depth_note: Responding to a state nexus questionnaire: voluntary disclosure vs wait-and-see
scenarios.prompt: I just got a nexus questionnaire from the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration. I've had about $120,000 in California sales over 3 years without collecting tax. Should I respond, do a voluntary disclosure, or ignore it? Lay out the risks, the VDA penalty waiver math, and the exact steps for each path.

scenarios.depth_note: SDE multiple valuation for a service business: add-backs, multiple ranges, buyer perspective
scenarios.prompt: I'm thinking about selling my marketing agency: $800,000 revenue, $220,000 in owner salary + profit. Value it using seller's discretionary earnings: walk me through the add-backs, what multiple a business like this actually sells for (and why), and what a buyer's first 3 objections will be.

scenarios.depth_note: 18-month value-building plan: reducing owner dependence, clean books, contract quality
scenarios.prompt: I want to sell my business in 18 months for maximum value. Right now I'm the rainmaker, the books are messy, and most clients are on handshake deals. Give me a prioritized 18-month plan: what to fix first, how much each fix typically moves the multiple, and what sale price difference we're talking about between selling now versus after the cleanup.
